subject: Private connector egress: registering customer IPs and firewall controls
messages:

Date: Mon, 14 Jun 2027 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Initial: private connector egress — IPs and firewall requirements

Hi Stephanie,

We're getting ready to onboard Redwood Private for our outpatient analytics cluster. Security wants a concrete list of source IPs and expected TLS endpoints so we can open firewall egress rules on our side. A few specifics from our side:

- We need a CSV with stable IPs or a documented fallback (if you only provide ephemeral ranges).
- Any required SNI or mTLS fingerprints we should match at the perimeter.
- A short runbook for what to update if Redwood rotates egress IPs.

Karen and I are the technical contacts. We also need to capture this in our procurement packet so please note any SLA/maintenance windows that might affect outbound connectivity.

Thanks,
Diego Hernandez
Security Engineer, Keystone Health

Subject: Re: Initial: private connector egress — IPs and firewall requirements

Diego — thanks for the clear ask. Looping in Laura, Marcus, and Kimberly to scope the technical approach.

Quick answers up front:
- We can support either (A) Redwood-managed fixed egress IP blocks for your environment, or (B) a customer-managed NAT/proxy with our private endpoint inside your VPC.
- We also support mutual TLS for the control plane and can provide SNI and certificate thumbprints if you choose that path.

Attached a CSV template for you to complete (ip-register-template.csv). Marcus can propose the default egress playbook and Kimberly will confirm policy constraints for fixed IPs.

Action: Diego/Karen — please fill the CSV and indicate if your security team requires certificate pinning or only SNI-level allowlist.

Best,
Stephanie Nguyen
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Initial: private connector egress — IPs and firewall requirements

Diego / team — outlining the two options with tradeoffs so Keystone can choose: 

Option A — Redwood-managed static egress blocks (recommended for ease of ops)
- We reserve dedicated outbound NAT IP blocks per-customer from our egress pool.
- We provide a signed CSV with /29 or /28 ranges (depends on throughput) and an expected rotation cadence (default: quarterly, with 30 days notice).
- We produce a short certificate thumbprint file for control-plane mTLS (optional).
- Pros: minimal customer infra changes, Redwood handles rotation and routing.
- Cons: requires Keystone to accept provider-owned static IPs in your perimeter policy.

Option B — Customer-managed NAT/proxy inside Keystone VPC (BYO NAT)
- Redwood's private endpoints will use the customer's egress path; you maintain the public IPs and rotation.
- We'll provide a required CIDR allocation for internal routing and a validation procedure for health checks.
- Pros: Keystone keeps IP ownership and rotation control.
- Cons: requires operations work on your side and adds troubleshooting steps for us if egress path fails.

Security controls we can provide regardless of option:
- SNI allowlist and certificate thumbprints (SHA256) for the control plane.
- TLS 1.2+ mandatory, optional mutual TLS for client/auth between control plane and private runtime.
- A runbook for emergency IP rotation and rollback (we'll include step-by-step commands, firewall rules to change, and a contact list).

I've attached a draft playbook (egress-orchestration-playbook-v1.md). Marcus Lin
Senior Infrastructure Engineer, Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Initial: private connector egress — IPs and firewall requirements

Thanks Marcus — a couple of policy points from Redwood's compliance side we need Keystone to acknowledge if you choose Option A: 

1) Rotation notice and SLA: Our default rotation cadence is quarterly; we provide a 30-day advance notice and a 72-hour emergency rotation window for security events. Roadmap customers can request longer notice windows under a dedicated capacity contract.

2) Audit evidence: We will provide logs showing observed outbound connections by IP and time window for a 90-day retention period (longer retention is an add-on).

3) IP ownership and redlines: Since Option A uses Redwood-managed IPs, the contract needs a clause that allows Redwood to advertise new egress ranges and that Keystone will accept those ranges into its perimeter as long as Redwood follows the rotation notice process.

If Keystone cannot accept provider-owned IPs in their perimeter policy, Option B (BYO NAT) is the required path.

Next steps (proposed):
- Diego/Karen: confirm preference (A or B) and return the completed CSV by EOD 2027-06-18.
- Redwood: we'll produce a small evidence packet (keystone-egress-sow.pdf) and a DocuSign for the ancillary clause if Option A is chosen.

Kimberly Park
Head of Product Security, Redwood Inference
From: Diego Hernandez <d.hernandez@keystonehealth.com>

Date: Fri, 18 Jun 2027 16:20:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Initial: private connector egress — IPs and firewall requirements

Thanks all — after internal review Keystone will proceed with Option A (Redwood-managed static egress blocks) provided the following are contractually agreed: 

- 30-day rotation notice (non-negotiable) and 72-hour emergency rotation window.
- Redwood provide SHA256 certificate thumbprints and an SNI allowlist.
- Redwood will include a 90-day outbound log retention for the project and deliver the initial evidence packet prior to Go-Live.

Attached the completed ip-register-template.csv (filled with our perimeter contact and ticketing info). We'll need the DocuSign clause for IP ownership to include in our procurement packet.

Please send the SOW and DocuSign link and we'll turn that around with procurement.

Best,
Diego Hernandez
Security Engineer, Keystone Health
